description: Alpine county (1003–1416, later duchy) controlling the western Alpine passes between France and Italy; its strategic position as gatekeeper of the Mont Cenis and Great St Bernard passes made it indispensable to both French and Italian powers, granting successive counts leverage far exceeding their modest territory to extract concessions and expand influence.

lifecycle_phases.description: Humbert I White-Handed establishes the dynasty controlling Alpine corridors.
Expansion into Bugey, Vaud, and northern Piedmont.
Amadeus VI the Green Count reaches maximum Savoyard extent.
Transition to duchy status under Amadeus VIII.

rise_factors.description: Control of the Alpine passes, Mont Cenis and Great St Bernard, made Savoy a strategic choke point on Italy-France routes.
Transit tolls on Alpine crossings funded Savoyard territorial expansion.
Systematic acquisition of Piedmontese lands through marriage, purchase, and inheritance.

Savoy controlled the most critical trans-Alpine passes (Mont Cenis, Great St. Bernard) connecting France and Italy. Pass tolls, combined with escort and hospitality services for travelers and armies, made these mountain passes the primary revenue source for Savoyard expansion.

Savoy's position between France and the Holy Roman Empire gave it permanent diplomatic leverage: both powers competed for Savoyard alliance, enabling successive dukes to extract territorial concessions and marriage alliances far beyond what military power would justify.

Amadeus VIII's elevation to Duke of Savoy (1416) and brief election as Antipope Felix V (1439–49) reflected Savoy's growing European status. The duchy controlled both sides of the Alps and constituted a minor European power.

Savoy controlled the Great St. Bernard and Mont Cenis passes linking France, Italy, and the Empire; transit tolls collected from pilgrims, merchants, and armies crossing the Alps financed the county's growth from a minor Burgundian fief to a major Alpine power.

decline_factors.description: Amadeus VIII faced challenges from the Achaean branch of the dynasty in the early 15th century.
County fragmented across Savoyard, Vaudois, and Piedmontese sub-domains requiring constant arbitration.

As France and the Italian states consolidated in the 15th century, Savoy's strategic position became a liability: it was repeatedly invaded, occupied, and forced to choose between larger neighbors. The 1536 French occupation of Piedmont demonstrated Savoy's structural vulnerability.
